headline: Nvidia beat and guided to $130 billion after a selloff that cost the Dow 849 points, while markets price a near-certain December hike and the 10-year sits at 5.10%.
dateline: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 · closes as of Tue Nov 17

rundown.h: Nvidia beats and guides to $130 billion.
rundown.p: In its first report since Jensen Huang's exit, Nvidia posted fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago, against about $109.1 billion expected, and adjusted EPS of $2.68. Data-center sales hit $107.6 billion. It guided to $130 billion next quarter while assuming no China data-center revenue, and gross margin guidance slipped to 71–72%. Shares rose 3% to 4% after hours.

rundown.h: Fed officials talk up more hikes before today's minutes.
rundown.p: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem floated as many as four more hikes before spring, New York Fed President John Williams stressed raising rates to contain inflation, and Cleveland's Beth Hammack favored small, gradual increases. Markets put roughly 96% odds on a quarter-point hike Dec. 9. Minutes of the Oct. 27–28 meeting, where two officials dissented in favor of a hike, land at 2 p.m. ET today.

Anthropic plans to sell 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, with pricing expected tonight and Nasdaq trading Thursday under ANT, subject to SEC effectiveness. At the $74 midpoint, net proceeds come to about $84.6 billion, including a $26 billion side sale of non-voting shares to seven tech companies. Pre-IPO contracts on Hyperliquid traded near $96.93 Monday, well above the range.

rundown.h: Chip curbs widen as Trump heads to meet Xi.
rundown.p: New U.S. rules now require licenses for advanced AI chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, and China said it will take necessary measures in response. ASML fell about 5% and Germany's DAX about 2%. President Trump is reported to meet Xi Jinping on Thursday in Shenzhen, so trade terms and chip access are both on the table.
rundown.src: Capital Street FX, citing Reuters and AP · Nov 18

rundown.h: Home Depot beats, and the retail parade continues.
rundown.p: Home Depot reported third-quarter sales of $43.4 billion, up 4.9%, and now sees full-year sales growth of about 4.5%, the top of its range, yet the stock fell 2.45%. CFO Richard McPhail becomes CEO on Nov. 23. Lowe's, Target and TJX report this morning and Walmart on Thursday, a read on how shoppers are handling high prices into the holidays.

dive.title: Freight's comeback runs on scarcity, not demand
dive.dek: Truckload rates are at or near records while volumes fall, because trucks and drivers are leaving the market.
dive.body:
After a long freight recession, trucking rates have roared back, but not because America is shipping more. DAT's October data show the dry-van spot rate averaged $3.05 a mile, the highest monthly figure since February 2022 and 98 cents above a year earlier, while van contract rates hit $3.28, matching the May 2022 record. Flatbed contract rates set a record for a third straight month at $4.05. Yet DAT's van volume index slipped 2% from a year ago. DAT's Dean Croke summed it up: brokers moved fewer loads and paid carriers about a dollar a mile more to move them (DAT, Nov 10).

The story is supply. Equipment posted on DAT's load board ran 22% to 26% below last year. Federal enforcement has revoked more than 28,000 non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses, and FMCSA expects about 194,000 holders to eventually exit the freight market (Transport Topics, May 7). Diesel adds a second squeeze: DAT estimated October's van fuel surcharge at 83 cents a mile, roughly double a year ago, which pushes small carriers out. ATA's Bob Costello has said the recovery is nearly all due to capacity leaving (FreightWaves, Oct 3).

The tightness is spreading to buildings. The Logistics Managers' Index for October showed warehousing prices at 80.7, up from 73.5, and transportation capacity contracting at 38 (Trading Economics, Nov 3). Survey respondents have been pulling durable-goods purchases forward on expected price increases, and tariff refunds are giving shippers a temporary lift.

Why it matters: higher freight costs feed goods inflation just as the Fed is hiking, but scarce trucks and scarce yard space support rents for truck terminals, trailer parking and well-located warehouses. What would change the picture: cheaper diesel if the Gulf calms, a court ruling against the license rules, or a demand slump once pre-buying fades and 5% rates bite.
watch: Early December: DAT's November spot and contract rates
Mondays: EIA diesel, the swing factor for small carriers

items.title: October retail sales rose 0.2%, matching forecasts, as the control group beat

chart.src: Source: Census Bureau via FRED (RSAFS, seasonally adjusted, current vintage), Nov 18

items.body:
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, in line with the consensus on Trading Economics, after 0.8% in September; August was revised up to 1.5%. Sales were up 6.8% from a year earlier. Ex-autos sales rose 0.6% against 0.4% expected, and the control group, which feeds GDP, rose 0.6%, above forecasts of 0.3% to 0.4% and its strongest gain since August.

Miscellaneous retailers jumped 4.7%, gas stations 1.5% and online sellers 1.2%. Car dealers fell 1.6%, furniture 2.3% and clothing 0.7%. Adjusted for inflation, volumes fell 0.1% (TD Economics), with consumer prices up 0.4% in October. Over the past 12 months, monthly gains ranged from −0.6% to 1.7%.

On the day, the 2-year Treasury yield slipped 3 basis points to 4.80% and the 10-year 2 basis points to 5.10% (Treasury), while futures held near 95% odds of a December hike.

experts.view: Called the report mixed: real volumes dipped, but the strong control group shows consumers enter the holidays in decent shape, with spending likely to cool as high rates weigh on housing and autos.
Noted the headline slowed but the details were strong, with upward revisions and solid three-month gains in core categories.

experts.who: Heather Long, chief economist, Navy Federal Credit Union
experts.view: Pointed out that inflation-adjusted spending fell and that many household budgets are stretched.

items.lean: TD and Haver read the details as solid; Navy Federal's Long stresses that real spending slipped.
items.src: Sources: Trading Economics; Haver Analytics; TD Economics; AP via PBS; Breitbart (control consensus); FRED; U.S. Treasury.

lead.title: The U.S. hits back near Hormuz as attacks on shipping rise
lead.body:
U.S. warplanes struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, on Nov. 17. A U.S. official called it a response to Iranian attacks on American personnel and assets, after Iran's third attack on Bahrain in under a week targeted a U.S. radar. Iran's Mehr News reported no casualties. A third U.S. carrier strike group arrived in the region Nov. 16 (gCaptain).

Bloomberg reports Iranian attacks on commercial vessels are rising. Parliament speaker and lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned Iran would hit civilian infrastructure near U.S. and Israeli bases if Iranian civilian sites are struck. Qatar, the main mediator, was due to meet Iranian representatives Nov. 17; neither side has moved on the U.S. naval blockade or nuclear terms.
lead.reach: Through oil: Brent settled at $93.14 on Nov 17, up 0.8%, and is up more than 50% this year (Xinhua; Bloomberg via Transport Topics). EIA data show Hormuz flows recovered to 9.1 million barrels a day in the third quarter, so new attacks threaten a recovery that markets had priced in.

views.who: Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist, TD Securities
views.view: Expects some geopolitical risk premium to be priced back into crude as tensions build and flows through the strait drop.
Continue to flag the risk of an oil glut next year, which would cap prices if flows hold up.

hot.chg: Nov 17: Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge for a second day and says a span collapsed; the Kremlin rejects a temporary ceasefire.
October inflation hit 4.0% (Italy 5.5%) after the ECB held its refi rate at 2.65% on Oct 29.
BoJ held at 1.25% on Oct 30 in an 8–1 vote; most economists in a Reuters poll expect 1.50% in December.
Nov 18: Bank Indonesia hiked 25 bp to 6.00%, following Australia's Nov 3 hike to 4.85%.

reading.title: Druckenmiller: read the central bank first
reading.dek: From a Pittsburgh bank trainee to Soros's partner on the sterling trade, Druckenmiller built one of the best long-run records in money management by betting on policy mistakes.
reading.body:
Before he became a byword for macro investing, Stanley Druckenmiller was an unlikely Wall Street candidate. Born in Pittsburgh on June 14, 1953, and raised in the Philadelphia suburbs, he studied English and economics at Bowdoin College, graduating in 1975. He then enrolled in the economics Ph.D. program at the University of Michigan but left partway through, a detour that pointed him toward markets rather than a lecture hall.

His first job, in 1977, was as a management trainee at Pittsburgh National Bank. Within roughly a year he was running its equity research group. In the early 1980s he struck out on his own, launching Duquesne Capital Management with a small pool of client money. Dreyfus took notice: he began consulting for the firm in 1985 and moved to New York in 1986 to manage the Dreyfus Fund, all while keeping Duquesne going.

In 1988 George Soros hired him to replace Victor Niederhoffer as lead portfolio manager of the Quantum Fund. The partnership produced the trade that made both men famous. In 1992 they bet heavily against the British pound, reasoning that the Bank of England lacked the reserves to defend its currency peg and that the rate hikes needed to do so would prove politically impossible. When sterling broke on Black Wednesday, the position reportedly earned more than $1 billion. His Soros years ended in 2000, after steep losses on technology stocks near the top of the dot-com bubble.

Duquesne, meanwhile, compiled one of the best long-run records in the industry, with average returns of about 30% a year from 1986. By 2010 it managed roughly $12 billion. That August he announced he would close the fund and return outside capital, citing the strain of running so much money and frustration that recent results trailed his own standard. He has since invested his own fortune through a family office and turned to philanthropy, giving $705 million to foundations in 2009 alone, including $100 million to found a neuroscience institute at NYU, and chairing Harlem Children's Zone.

The through-line of his career is a habit of reading central banks and liquidity first, then sizing positions boldly when the evidence lines up, and cutting them quickly when it does not. The sterling trade was less a gamble than a judgment that policymakers had boxed themselves in. His 2000 stumble is the counterweight: even the best macro thinkers can get caught chasing a mania.

quote.src: Stanley Druckenmiller on closing Duquesne Capital, 2010 (via InvestmentNews)

takeaways: With a Dec. 9 hike nearly priced, the Fed's path still drives every asset.
A 5.10% 10-year and a strong dollar mean liquidity is tightening, not loosening.
When a crowded bet turns, cut it fast rather than chase momentum.
